'You skipped lab again,' Eshaan said, sliding a cutting chai across the canteen table.
'Went home. Mummy needed help at the shop.' Charu didn't look up. 'It's fine.'
'That's the third Friday.'
'I said it's fine.'
Eshaan waited. The fan ticked overhead.
'The research internship form closes on Monday,' Charu said finally. 'Papa thinks I should come home after graduation and help run things. And I want to go to Pune for this. And I'm so tired of being the good one in both places.'
'That sounds exhausting.'
'Aren't you going to tell me what to do? Everyone else does.'
'Nope. I'll just ask: what do you want, if nobody's watching?'
Charu stirred the chai for a long time. 'I don't know yet. Can I think out loud at you for a bit?'
'Take all evening.'

qa.a: The form closes on Monday.

qa.q: What does Charu repeating 'It's fine' suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Charu is worn out and dodging the topic, holding in stress about the pull from home and the internship.

qa.q: What choice did Eshaan make when Charu asked to be told what to do?
qa.a: Eshaan chose not to push either side and asked what Charu wants if nobody's watching, which gave Charu room to think out loud.

qa.q: What is it like for Charu to be 'the good one' in both places?
qa.a: It seems draining for Charu to keep meeting home's hopes while chasing the internship, with nowhere to simply be honest.

grounding: Shows Eshaan noticing Charu tired and evasive between family expectations and personal goals, and listening without pushing either side.

subtype: Observing a friend caught between worlds [Observer]

Last winter I watched Jatin get thinner and quieter. He'd come to our flat for group study and fall asleep on the rug, or stare at his phone every time it buzzed and not answer. When I asked if he was okay, he'd say 'just tired' and switch to talking about exams.
One night he admitted it. His family wanted him to take over the coaching centre his father built. He had secretly done three weekend shifts in a restaurant kitchen and felt, for the first time, like himself.
I badly wanted to say 'follow your dream!' like a poster on a wall. I didn't. I just asked questions and made him tea.
Months later he told me, 'Pooja, you're the only one who didn't pick a side. That's why I could finally hear myself.'

qa.q: Where had Jatin secretly done three weekend shifts?
qa.a: In a restaurant kitchen.

qa.q: What did Pooja want to say when Jatin finally admitted it, and why hold back?
qa.a: Pooja was eager to cheer 'follow your dream!', but held back and just asked questions and made tea, not wanting to pick a side.

qa.q: Why was Pooja's choice to hold back the 'follow your dream' line a good one?
qa.a: Holding back and just asking questions gave Jatin room to think without one more person pushing, so he could finally hear himself.

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Pooja just asks questions instead of picking a side?
qa.a: Jatin likely felt relieved and less pushed, with room to hear his own thoughts, as he later told Pooja.

grounding: Shows Pooja noticing Jatin tired and evasive while caught between family expectations and a personal goal, and helping by listening without taking sides.

Peer-mentor log, week six. Akash cancelled our Tuesday study session again, the third time. When I found him in the canteen he looked grey with tiredness. He said his father wants him home every weekend to help at the shop, while his own plan is to prepare for the civil services exam with a group here. "I'm fine, just busy," he said, and changed the subject to cricket. I didn't push him to pick a side. I said, "You don't have to decide anything with me. I'm just here if you want to think out loud." Twenty minutes later he did, slowly. Next step: we'll meet on Thursday at the same table, no agenda.
Baljeet

Wednesday. Something's off with Vishal. He used to be first at our Sunday photography walks; he's missed four in a row. Today he said he was "just tired" and looked at his phone the whole lunch. I know his parents want him to join the family textile business in Surat after graduation, and I know he's secretly applying for a design master's. When I asked, he said, "Don't start." So I didn't. I just told him I'd be at the tea stall after class if he wanted to talk, about anything or nothing. He came. He didn't talk about Surat. He talked about how tired he was of being two people. I mostly listened. It felt like the right thing.
Indu

subtype: Observing a friend caught between worlds [Observer]
passage:
Every evening Asif waited for the last bus back from the district college with Vinita. This month, she had changed.
She used to chatter about her teaching course and the school she wanted to start in their village. Now she dozed against the window, dark circles under her eyes. When he asked how the wedding talks at home were going, she said, "Fine," and looked away.
Asif noticed she'd missed two assignments. He also noticed her mother calling three times a day.
One evening, as the bus bumped past the sugarcane fields, he said, "You don't have to tell me anything. But if you want to think out loud, I'll just listen. No advice."
She was quiet for a long time. Then: "They want me married by winter. I want to finish the course. I don't know how to hold both."
Asif nodded and said nothing, and she kept talking until their stop.

qa.q: What did Vinita want to start in their village?
qa.a: A school.

qa.q: How did Asif feel as he watched Vinita change?
qa.a: He was concerned for her, noticing how tired and evasive she had become, and wanted to help without pushing.

qa.q: Why did Asif's offer to just listen work?
qa.a: It gave Vinita space to think aloud without being pulled toward either her family's plan or her course, so she could speak freely.

qa.q: What is it like for Vinita to be caught between wedding plans and her course?
qa.a: She is exhausted and torn, not knowing how to hold both, which shows in her dozing, missed assignments and short answers.

grounding: Shows a friend noticing a tired, evasive peer caught between family expectations and her goals, and offering to listen without taking sides.
